fields.epidemiology: Homeless individuals, refugees, victims of war and natural disasters, people in crowded living conditions with poor hygiene
fields.risk_factors: Inability to wash or change clothes (lets the infestation persist); crowded living conditions; poor hygiene
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pruritus; linear excoriations mainly on the back, neck, shoulders and waist; postinflammatory pigmentation in chronic cases
fields.diagnosis: Close examination of the seams of clothing for nits; shaking clothing over white paper (lice move on the paper)
fields.treatment: Multimodal approach (resistance is rising): topical pediculicides (pyrethrins, permethrin, malathion, spinosad, ivermectin); effect read 24 hours after application; then clean clothing, and dry (unwashed) or bag for 2 weeks all clothing, bedding and towels from the prior week

fields.name: Pediculosis pubis (also: crabs)
fields.definition: Parasitic infestation of the pubic area by the pubic (crab) louse
fields.etiology: Phthirus pubis: 0.8-1.2 mm with a wide, short, crab-like body; spread sexually, also via contaminated clothing, towels, bedding
fields.epidemiology: Found in all levels of society and ethnic groups; patients often have a concurrent sexually transmitted disease
fields.risk_factors: Sexual contact; shared clothing, towels or bedding
fields.pathology: Maculae caerulae represent hemorrhage; papular urticaria forms at feeding sites
fields.clinical: Often asymptomatic or mild-moderate pruritus for months; maculae caerulae (slate-gray to bluish irregular macules about 1 cm); papular urticaria, often periumbilical; eyelash infestation (pediculosis or phthiriasis palpebrarum)
fields.diagnosis: Nits at the base of hairs; confirmed by microscopic examination of a plucked hair
fields.treatment: Multimodal approach (resistance is rising): topical pediculicides (pyrethrins, permethrin, malathion, spinosad, ivermectin); effect read 24 hours after application; then clean clothing, and dry (unwashed) or bag for 2 weeks all clothing, bedding and towels from the prior week

fields.name: Bedbug bites
fields.definition: Bites from bedbugs, nocturnal blood-feeding insects that hide by day in cracks and crevices
fields.etiology: Cimex lectularius (common bedbug) and Cimex pilosellus (batbug)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Clothing and baggage of travelers and visitors; secondhand mattresses; laundry
fields.pathology: Hide in headboards, picture frames, behind loose wallpaper; feed at night, drawn by warmth and carbon dioxide; need a blood meal every 5-10 days but survive up to 1 year; can shed pathogens (hepatitis B) but no convincing evidence they act as vectors
fields.clinical: Painless, multiple bites grouped in a line; a row of 3 = breakfast, lunch, and dinner; wheals and papules with a hemorrhagic punctum; bullous in sensitized patients; blood flecks on bed linens
fields.diagnosis: Physical examination
fields.treatment: Symptomatic treatment and local wound care; secondary infection: topical antiseptic lotion or antibiotic cream; pruritus: topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines; professional exterminator needed to eradicate

fields.name: Tungiasis and flea bites (also: fleas)
fields.definition: Tungiasis: infestation by penetration of the adult female flea (family Tungidae) into human skin to lay eggs; Pulicidae fleas cause papular bite reactions
fields.etiology: Wingless blood-sucking fleas that jump up to 18 cm; Tungidae cause tungiasis; rat fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis, Xenopsylla brasiliensis) transmit bubonic plague; cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) carries bubonic plague and endemic typhus
fields.epidemiology: Tungiasis endemic in the West Indies, Central America, Africa, India, Pakistan, South America
fields.risk_factors: Travel to or residence in endemic areas; walking barefoot or in sandals on beaches, sitting in sand (Nigeria, the Caribbean, India, Brazil)
fields.pathology: Flea bite reactions scale with sensitization: urticarial papules (non-sensitized), papular urticaria (sensitized), bullae (hypersensitive)
fields.clinical: Tungiasis: papules enlarging over weeks to 4-10 mm, firm yellow translucent nodule, may be painful; plantar feet, subungual/periungual skin, web spaces, legs; pain, pruritus, autoamputation of toes · flea bites: linear or clustered urticarial papules, usually lower legs
fields.diagnosis: Dermoscopy showing ovoid eggs (tungiasis)
fields.treatment: Surgical excision, or cryotherapy/topical agents; tetanus prophylaxis; systemic antibiotics; prevention: avoid going barefoot or in sandals on beaches in endemic areas

fields.name: Hymenoptera stings (also: bees, wasps, fire ants)
fields.definition: Stings from bees, wasps and ants, insects with poison glands for defense or hunting
fields.etiology: Stings inflicted by female insects through a modified ovipositor (egg-laying apparatus) when the nest or insect is threatened; fire ants attack in groups
fields.epidemiology: Generalized systemic reactions in 0.4-3%
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Honeybee barbed stinger stays impaled and keeps pumping venom; fire ant venom triggers mast cell degranulation (flushing, pruritus, hives, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)
fields.clinical: Typical: immediate burning pain, then intense local erythema, swelling, urticaria · severe local: extensive edema and induration up to 1 week · systemic: anaphylaxis (generalized urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm)
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Remove stinger fast by scraping with a credit card edge or dull knife parallel to the skin; mild: cleaning, ice, local anesthetic injection; anaphylaxis: subcutaneous or intramuscular epinephrine, emergency room; hypersensitive patients carry an EpiPen; desensitization, immunotherapy for fire ants

fields.name: Caterpillar dermatitis (also: lepidopterism; erucism)
fields.definition: Lepidopterism: the aggregate medical effects of caterpillars, moths and butterflies; erucism (caterpillar dermatitis) is the gypsy moth caterpillar form
fields.etiology: About 100-150 species; gypsy moth, processionary and asp (puss) caterpillars
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Mechanical irritation by pointed hairs; toxin injection through hollow hairs; cell-mediated hypersensitivity to hairs
fields.clinical: Varies by species: gypsy moth: pruritic erythematous papules in linear streaks · processionary: urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis · asp or puss caterpillar (most poisonous): intense painful sting, train-track purpura
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Remove hairs by stripping with adhesive tape; symptomatic: systemic antihistamines, topical menthol or camphor, moderate-high potency topical corticosteroids, systemic corticosteroids, oral or parenteral narcotic analgesics; antivenom for certain categories

fields.name: Cutaneous larva migrans
fields.definition: Syndrome in which larvae of animal nematodes infect humans, who are a dead-end host
fields.etiology: Animal hookworm larvae, mostly from dogs and cats; infection requires contact with sand or soil contaminated with animal feces
fields.epidemiology: Tropical and subtropical areas: southeastern United States, Caribbean, Africa, Central and South America, India, Southeast Asia
fields.risk_factors: Skin contact with sand or soil contaminated with animal feces
fields.pathology: Larvae trapped in the follicular canal, stratum corneum or dermis with an inflammatory eosinophilic infiltrate
fields.clinical: Classic: erythematous, raised, vesicular, linear or serpentine track advancing 2-3 cm/day; intense pruritus and pain; lasts 2-8 weeks; often feet and buttocks; systemic signs rare · hookworm folliculitis: follicular papules and pustules, usually the buttock
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Clinical diagnosis]] when the serpiginous rash is present; light microscopy with mineral oil shows live and dead larvae (in folliculitis)
fields.treatment: [[★ Albendazole]] 400 mg by mouth daily for 3 days, or ivermectin for 1-2 days; hookworm folliculitis may need repeated treatment; topical therapy less effective; excision or cryotherapy not recommended

fields.name: Black widow spider bite
fields.definition: Envenomation by the black widow spider, marked by a red hourglass on the underside of the abdomen
fields.etiology: Latrodectus mactans (southern black widow); bites follow accidental or deliberate provocation
fields.epidemiology: Found in all but the most northern part of the country; webs in corners of doors and windows, woodpiles, garages, sheds, outdoor toilet seats
fields.risk_factors: Higher risk of complications in the very old, very young, or those with cardiovascular disease
fields.pathology: Venom contains the neurotoxin alpha-latrotoxin
fields.clinical: Painful bite, mild skin findings; within 30 minutes local erythema, piloerection, sweating; agonizing crampy abdominal pain and muscle spasms; headache, paresthesia, nausea, vomiting, hypertension, lacrimation, salivation, seizures, tremors, acute renal failure, paralysis
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Local wound care or hospitalization depending on symptoms; envenomation: calcium gluconate 10%, narcotic analgesics, muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines; ensure tetanus vaccine is up to date

fields.name: Brown recluse spider bite
fields.definition: Bite of the brown recluse spider, ranging from mild local reactions to severe ulcerative necrosis
fields.etiology: Loxosceles reclusa: non-aggressive spider with a dark brown fiddle/violin marking on the cephalothorax; bites when threatened or provoked
fields.epidemiology: Abundant in the American Midwest and Southeast; shelters in undisturbed places (closets, attics, stored bedding and clothing)
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: In a small percentage, the wound progresses to necrosis (days 2-3), eschar (days 5-7), then deep ulcers
fields.clinical: [[★ Hallmark]]: red, white, and blue sign (central violaceous area, rim of blanched skin, surrounding large asymmetric area); systemic symptoms 1-2 days after the bite: nausea, vomiting, headache, fever, chills
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Pain control, warm compresses, avoid strenuous exercise; antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection; slow-healing necrotic wounds may need surgical reconstruction, delayed until the wound is stable

fields.name: Hobo spider bite (also: aggressive house spider)
fields.definition: Bite of the hobo spider, the predominant cause of necrotic arachnidism in the Pacific Northwest
fields.etiology: Tegenaria agrestis, the [[★ aggressive house spider]]: brown with a gray herringbone pattern on the abdomen; often mistaken for the brown recluse
fields.epidemiology: Pacific Northwest of the United States; bites July to September (mating season); webs in basements, wood piles, bushes
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Painless bite; induration and paresthesia within 30 minutes; large erythematous area; vesicles in the first 36 hours; sometimes eschar; systemic: headache, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, paresthesia, memory impairment
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Supportive measures; wounds heal within several weeks; headaches may last up to 1 week
fields.mortality: Rarely fatal from severe systemic effects, including aplastic anemia

fields.name: Tarantula hair reaction
fields.definition: Skin and eye reactions to tarantula hairs that land and embed when the tarantula is threatened
fields.etiology: Tarantulas (family Theraphosidae)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Embedded hairs provoke responses from mild local pruritus to granulomatous reactions
fields.clinical: Generally mild and local: pruritus to granulomatous skin reactions; eye: conjunctivitis, corneal granuloma
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Topical corticosteroids for skin reactions; ophthalmology consult for ocular involvement

fields.name: Lyme disease
fields.definition: Tick-borne illness caused by a spirochete, progressing through early localized, early disseminated and late persistent stages
fields.etiology: Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete), carried by Ixodes ticks (I. scapularis, I. pacificus, I. ricinus, I. persulcatus)
fields.epidemiology: Northern hemisphere (North America, Europe, Asia); in the United States: Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Wisconsin
fields.risk_factors: Living in or travel to an endemic region
fields.pathology: Ticks feed on animals that maintain the organism, then pass it on by transstadial transmission (from one tick life stage to the next); birds and deer disperse it
fields.clinical: Stage 1 (about 1 week): erythema migrans (bull's-eye: over 5 cm, expanding, central clearing, darker punctate center), fever, myalgia, arthralgia · Stage 2 (days-weeks): cranial nerve palsies, meningitis, radiculopathy, arthritis · Stage 3 (months-years): mono/oligoarthritis of knee, encephalopathy, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans
fields.diagnosis: Erythema migrans: diagnose and treat clinically · other presentations: two-tier serology, ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) for IgM (immunoglobulin M) and IgG (immunoglobulin G), the IgG C6 peptide test being more specific, then confirm with Western blot; testing most useful outside endemic regions
fields.treatment: Remove tick immediately; antibiotics in all stages: doxycycline first line, amoxicillin for early erythema migrans, azithromycin second line, 10-14 days · intravenous ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or penicillin G if oral not tolerated, early disseminated or late neurologic disease, recurrent arthritis · repellents; no human vaccine

fields.name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
fields.definition: Tick-borne rickettsial illness with a classic triad of fever, headache and rash
fields.etiology: Rickettsia rickettsii; vectors: dog tick, wood tick, rodents; incubation 3-12 days
fields.epidemiology: Southeastern and South Central states, in spring and early summer
fields.risk_factors: Male sex; adults 40-64 years; children under 10 years; rural dwelling
fields.pathology: Delayed or inadequate treatment leads to severe cardiac, gastrointestinal, hepatic, neurologic, ophthalmologic, renal and pulmonary manifestations; long-term sequelae in severe-disease survivors
fields.clinical: Triad (only about 60%): fever over 39.5 °C, headache, rash; rash 2-4 days after fever, starts at wrists and ankles, spreads centripetally, involves palms and soles, spares face; blanching macules becoming petechiae and purpura; about 20% have no rash; abdominal pain mimics appendicitis in children
fields.diagnosis: Labs: thrombocytopenia, anemia, mild hyponatremia, mild transaminase elevation, normal white count with increased bands · IFA (indirect immunofluorescence assay) is the gold standard but rarely positive before day 7, so start treatment while awaiting results
fields.treatment: Doxycycline by mouth every 12 hours for 5-10 days in adults, pregnancy and children (weight-based); allergy: doxycycline desensitization; start by day 5; no prophylactic antibiotics; prevention: avoid ticks, protective clothing, tick checks, DEET (diethyltoluamide)

fields.name: Cercarial dermatitis (also: schistosome dermatitis; swimmer's itch; clam digger's itch)
fields.definition: Acute pruritic eruption from skin penetration by cercariae (free-swimming larval stage) of certain parasitic flatworms
fields.etiology: Fluke cercariae: host animal (waterfowl, marsh birds, finches, muskrats, mice, deer) passes eggs into water, which infect a snail within 12 hours; cercariae released after 5 weeks and carried to shore by wind and currents
fields.epidemiology: Great Lakes region; paddy workers and rice farmers of the Far East
fields.risk_factors: Exposure to cercaria-infested water; paddy and rice farming
fields.pathology: Cercariae penetrate the epidermis and dermis, then blood vessels, intrahepatic veins and intestinal walls
fields.clinical: Urticaria-like lesions and prickling about 30 minutes after exposure; severe pruritus 10-12 hours later; erythematous papules within 24 hours becoming vesicles then pustules; pain and swelling peak at 48-72 hours; sometimes headache, fever, lymphangitis
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Symptomatic: antihistamines, oatmeal baths, antipruritic lotions, aspirin for pain, washing and hygiene, topical or oral glucocorticoids

fields.name: Tinea capitis (also: ringworm of the scalp; black dot tinea capitis)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte (tinea) infection of the scalp and hair shaft.
fields.etiology: Trichophyton and Microsporum; Trichophyton tonsurans most common in the United States. Spread by infected people, pets, fallen hairs, clothing, combs, hats, furniture; asymptomatic carriers.
fields.epidemiology: Predominantly preadolescent children; most common fungal infection in children.
fields.risk_factors: Contact with infected persons, pets or shared fomites (combs, brushes, hats, towels); fungal particles stay viable for months.
fields.pathology: Dermatophytes survive only on dead keratin (stratum corneum, hair, nails); after puberty, changed fatty acid content of sebum is believed to inhibit growth.
fields.clinical: Pruritus; alopecia common (not in all cases); red papules progressing to grayish ring-formed scaly patches with perifollicular papules; black dot form (hairs broken at the scalp surface); lymphadenopathy often; kerion may develop (may have purulent drainage).
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy and fungal culture when feasible, especially before prolonged systemic therapy; Wood lamp may support Microsporum (Trichophyton tonsurans usually does not fluoresce); bacterial culture if a kerion drains pus. Differential: folliculitis, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, alopecia areata.
fields.treatment: Oral therapy required (topicals do not penetrate the hair shaft): terbinafine for Trichophyton, griseofulvin for Microsporum; [[★ obtain baseline liver tests]] when indicated. Adjunct selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo; no sharing hair items; complete course; treat inflammation promptly to limit scarring alopecia.

fields.name: Tinea barbae (also: ringworm of the beard)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte infection of the beard area.
fields.etiology: Trichophyton species common; inflammatory form usually acquired from animals (zoophilic), noninflammatory form usually from another person (anthropophilic).
fields.epidemiology: Rare.
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic or mild pruritus. Inflammatory: tender, boggy, pustular, kerion-like plaques, loose easily removed hairs, possible scarring alopecia. Noninflammatory: annular scaly plaques or folliculitis-like eruption; hairs break near the surface.
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy, culture; biopsy for refractory cases. Differential: bacterial folliculitis (hair easily removed in tinea barbae, not in bacterial folliculitis; bacterial culture to rule out), acne, rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis.
fields.treatment: Oral antifungal required (topicals do not penetrate the follicle): griseofulvin or terbinafine; [[★ baseline liver tests before oral antifungals]]. Shave or remove hair; warm compresses to remove crusts.

fields.name: Tinea corporis (also: ringworm of the body)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte infection of the body skin.
fields.etiology: Trichophyton rubrum common pathogen; contact with infected humans or animals.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Contact with infected humans or animals (ask about cats, dogs, kids); topical steroid or steroid-combination use can mask and worsen it.
fields.pathology: Dermatophyte living on dead keratin of the stratum corneum; progressive central clearing produces the annular outline.
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic or pruritic; one or more circular, sharply circumscribed, slightly erythematous, dry scaly patches/plaques with central clearing (annular "ringworm"); sharper outer ring than nummular eczema.
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy from the active border; culture if high suspicion with negative KOH or refractory; species and susceptibility testing if resistance suspected. Differential: psoriasis, nummular eczema (KOH negative), discoid lupus, fixed drug eruption.
fields.treatment: Localized: topical terbinafine, butenafine or an azole to the lesion and 1-2 cm beyond; avoid steroid-antifungal combinations. Oral (terbinafine; itraconazole or fluconazole) for extensive, follicular, immunocompromised, refractory or recurrent disease.

fields.name: Tinea cruris (also: jock itch)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte infection of the inguinal creases (crural fold).
fields.etiology: Most often Trichophyton rubrum and Epidermophyton floccosum.
fields.epidemiology: More common in men; often coexists with tinea pedis.
fields.risk_factors: Warm, moist environment; obesity; diabetes; tight-fitting clothes for long periods; sharing clothes.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pruritic, sharply demarcated plaque on the proximal medial thigh; scrotum typically spared.
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy from the active border in uncertain cases. Differential: candidal intertrigo (involves scrotum, satellite papules/pustules), erythrasma (may fluoresce coral-red).
fields.treatment: Topical allylamine (terbinafine) or azole (ketoconazole); oral only for extensive/refractory disease. Treat coexisting tinea pedis, keep folds dry, avoid steroid combination products.

fields.name: Tinea pedis (also: athlete's foot; interdigital, hyperkeratotic (shoe distribution) and vesiculobullous forms)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte infection of the feet; three variants: interdigital, hyperkeratotic, vesiculobullous (inflammatory).
fields.etiology: Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton interdigitale or Epidermophyton floccosum; spread by contact with infected desquamated skin.
fields.epidemiology: Most common dermatophyte infection in adults; men more than women.
fields.risk_factors: Warm, moist environment: shoes, locker room floors, sweating; immunocompromise.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Scaling, pruritus, burning or stinging; hands may be infected too. Interdigital (most common): maceration, erosions, scale and fissures between toes, especially 3rd-4th web space. Hyperkeratotic: plantar scale to diffuse thickening in a shoe distribution. Vesiculobullous: painful vesicles/bullae on erythema.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy from advancing scale if uncertain; culture for atypical, recurrent, severe or refractory disease; bacterial studies if marked maceration, malodor, drainage or cellulitis. Differential: candidiasis/mixed toe web infection, contact dermatitis, psoriasis.
fields.treatment: Topical terbinafine/butenafine or an azole; keratolytic (salicylic acid, lactic acid, urea) plus antifungal for hyperkeratotic; oral for extensive, recurrent, refractory or immunocompromised. Treat coexisting onychomycosis; dry between toes, sandals in showers, change socks, antifungal powder.

fields.name: Onychomycosis (also: tinea unguium)
fields.definition: Fungal infection of the nail; forms: distal lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, endonyx, total dystrophic.
fields.etiology: Dermatophytes, especially Trichophyton rubrum, cause most cases; yeasts and molds also occur.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Tinea pedis, age, diabetes, trauma, occlusive footwear, psoriasis, vascular disease.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Distal lateral disease: subungual debris, onycholysis, thickening, discoloration, crumbling.
fields.diagnosis: Confirm fungus before oral therapy (many dystrophic nails are not fungal): KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy, PAS (periodic acid-Schiff) stain of clippings, fungal culture or PCR (polymerase chain reaction); sample the most proximal diseased nail bed/subungual debris.
fields.treatment: Oral terbinafine first-line: about 6 weeks fingernails, 12 weeks toenails; [[★ baseline liver tests]] per labeling and risk. Itraconazole alternative (fluconazole off label). Limited disease: topical efinaconazole, tavaborole or ciclopirox (lower cure). Needs nail growth; treat tinea pedis.

fields.name: Tinea manuum (also: two feet-one hand syndrome)
fields.definition: Dermatophyte infection of the hand.
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Associated with tinea pedis; palms and soles may be infected at the same time.
fields.risk_factors: Coexisting tinea pedis; the hand used to scratch the feet is affected (two feet-one hand syndrome).
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Often unnoticed (blamed on dry skin or labor). Dorsum: annular plaque like tinea corporis. Palm: thickened, dry, scaly (hyperkeratotic) like tinea pedis; high recurrence.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Same as tinea pedis: topical terbinafine/butenafine or an azole; keratolytic plus antifungal for hyperkeratotic; oral for extensive, recurrent, refractory or immunocompromised; treat coexisting onychomycosis; moisture control.

fields.name: Id reaction (also: dermatophytid or identity reaction)
fields.definition: Inflammatory dermatitis at sites distant from a primary dermatophyte infection.
fields.etiology: Occurs with any dermatophyte infection; tinea pedis common.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Unknown; possibly delayed-type hypersensitivity.
fields.clinical: 1-2 weeks after primary infection; extremely pruritic papules or papulovesicles, common on fingers; toe webs may show an asymptomatic fissure or maceration (tinea pedis).
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) positive at the primary site, negative at the id site. Three criteria: dermatophyte infection elsewhere; no fungal elements at the id site; resolution once the primary infection is treated.
fields.treatment: Treat the primary dermatophyte infection; the id reaction then resolves.

fields.name: Tinea incognito
fields.definition: Tinea with a clinically altered appearance due to inappropriate treatment, usually topical steroids.
fields.etiology: Topical steroids used for anything inflammatory; steroid-antifungal combinations (clotrimazole/betamethasone dipropionate) are a common cause; calcineurin inhibitors also.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Steroids mask and worsen dermatophytosis; when stopped the lesion flares, prompting more steroid.
fields.clinical: Altered-looking tinea that flares when steroids are stopped; inflammation may rebound after withdrawal.
fields.diagnosis: KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation and/or culture from an active edge.
fields.treatment: Stop the corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor; topical antifungal for localized disease, systemic for extensive, follicular or refractory infection.

fields.name: Cutaneous candidiasis (candidal intertrigo) (also: intertrigo)
fields.definition: Yeast infection of the skin; intertrigo is an inflammatory rash from friction, moisture and heat in body folds that Candida may secondarily infect.
fields.etiology: Yeast; Candida albicans most common; opportunistic organism.
fields.epidemiology: Males equal females.
fields.risk_factors: Obesity, diabetes, incontinence, occlusion, immobility, recent antibiotics, immunosuppression.
fields.pathology: Yeasts are unicellular fungi that reproduce by budding and live on moist surfaces.
fields.clinical: Pruritus, burning pain; well-demarcated erythematous patches of varying sizes with [[★ satellite lesions (papules/pustules)]] (small red bumps just outside the main rash edge); inframammary, axillary, abdominal, inguinal, perineal, interdigital folds; commonly involves the scrotum.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation; culture. Malodor, erosions or drainage raise concern for bacterial coinfection.
fields.treatment: Dry folds, reduce friction/occlusion, manage incontinence. Topical nystatin (Candida only) or azole (Candida and dermatophytes); brief low-potency steroid only with antifungal. Recurrent/extensive: evaluate for diabetes, immunosuppression, resistance, alternative diagnosis.

fields.name: Pityriasis versicolor (also: tinea versicolor)
fields.definition: Overgrowth of normal skin yeast causing hypopigmented, hyperpigmented or pink finely scaling macules/patches.
fields.etiology: Lipid-dependent Malassezia species that normally inhabit skin; not considered contagious.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Heat, humidity, oily skin, sweating, immunosuppression, corticosteroid exposure; warm climates.
fields.pathology: Hypopigmentation from altered melanocyte function and reduced tanning; hyperpigmentation/erythema from inflammation and stratum corneum change.
fields.clinical: Usually asymptomatic or mild pruritus; velvety tan, pink or white scaling macules 4-5 mm to confluent areas on trunk, neck, upper arms, groin; recurrence common.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; scrape to reveal fine scale; KOH (potassium hydroxide): short hyphae and yeast clusters, "spaghetti and meatballs"; Wood lamp yellow-gold (limited). Differential: seborrheic dermatitis, pityriasis rosea, vitiligo.
fields.treatment: Topical first-line: ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione, ciclopirox or topical terbinafine. Oral fluconazole/itraconazole if extensive/refractory; oral terbinafine ineffective; [[★ never oral ketoconazole]] (hepatic, adrenal toxicity). Pigment lags scale.

fields.name: Varicella (also: chickenpox)
fields.definition: Primary varicella-zoster virus infection: a generalized pruritic eruption with lesions in multiple stages of healing.
fields.etiology: Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus; exposure to vesicular fluid (or airborne virus from disseminated zoster) in a susceptible person can cause varicella.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Susceptible people (no evidence of immunity); complication risk rises in adults, pregnancy, newborn age and immunocompromise.
fields.pathology: Contagious from 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions crust (breakthrough disease without crusts: until no new lesions for 24 hours); virus then stays latent in cranial-nerve or dorsal-root ganglia.
fields.clinical: Pruritic eruption evolving macules → papules → vesicles → crusts, with several stages present simultaneously; concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face.
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; lesion PCR (polymerase chain reaction) preferred when confirmation is needed; a reportable disease (Florida Department of Health).
fields.treatment: Supportive; avoid aspirin in children, caution with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; early oral antivirals if higher risk; intravenous acyclovir if severe/disseminated; prompt consult for pregnancy, neonatal exposure, immunocompromise. Prevention: two-dose vaccine; airborne and contact precautions.

fields.name: Herpes zoster (also: shingles)
fields.definition: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus causing neuropathic pain and a usually unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption.
fields.etiology: Varicella-zoster virus latent in cranial-nerve or dorsal-root ganglia reactivates as virus-specific cellular immunity wanes.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Increasing age; impaired cell-mediated immunity.
fields.pathology: Reactivated virus travels along a sensory nerve to the skin; each spinal nerve supplies one side only. Contagious (about one third as much as varicella) to non-immune contacts, who get varicella, not shingles; infectious until lesions dry.
fields.clinical: Prodrome of dermatomal pain/dysesthesia, lesions by 48–72 hours; then grouped herpetiform vesicles on an erythematous base in one or two adjacent dermatomes that [[★ does not cross midline]]; thoracic 55%; crusts; heals in 10–15 days; zoster sine herpete (pain without rash).
fields.diagnosis: Typical unilateral dermatomal vesicles: clinical; PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of vesicle fluid, scab or lesion-base cells for atypical, disseminated, vaccine-modified or immunocompromised cases. Differential: herpes simplex, contact dermatitis, impetigo, varicella.
fields.treatment: Oral valacyclovir, famciclovir or acyclovir ideally within 72 hours (later if new lesions or complicated); intravenous acyclovir if severe/sight-threatening; analgesics, cool compresses; [[★ corticosteroids do not prevent postherpetic neuralgia]]; Shingrix 2 doses at ≥50 years (≥19 if immunosuppressed).

fields.name: Postherpetic neuralgia
fields.definition: Zoster pain persisting ≥ 90 days after rash onset.
fields.etiology: Injury of peripheral nerves by herpes zoster.
fields.epidemiology: The most common complication of herpes zoster.
fields.risk_factors: Older age, severe acute pain, severe rash, ophthalmic involvement, immunocompromise.
fields.pathology: Neuropathic pain resulting from injury of peripheral nerves.
fields.clinical: Burning, aching, stabbing, shooting or electric shock–like pain, or allodynia (pain evoked by light touch); very debilitating; may last months to years, impairing sleep, mood and function.
fields.diagnosis: Pain persisting ≥ 90 days after zoster rash onset (the commonly used definition).
fields.treatment: First line: gabapentin/pregabalin, a tricyclic antidepressant, or topical lidocaine; capsaicin patch may help; individualize for kidney function, falls, interactions; avoid routine long-term opioids; refer severe pain. [[★ Corticosteroids do not prevent postherpetic neuralgia]].

fields.name: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
fields.definition: Herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic division (V1) of cranial nerve V.
fields.etiology: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (herpes zoster) in the V1 distribution.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Hutchinson sign (lesions on the tip/side of the nose) raises ocular risk, but its absence does not exclude eye involvement; eye pain, visual symptoms, red eye, photophobia, eyelid/ocular lesions; urgent, can cause blindness.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; evaluate urgently for ophthalmic disease.
fields.treatment: Start systemic antiviral therapy immediately; intravenous acyclovir with specialist care for sight-threatening disease; same-day ophthalmology evaluation for eye symptoms, Hutchinson sign or eyelid/ocular involvement.

fields.name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (also: herpes zoster oticus)
fields.definition: Herpes zoster of the ear: peripheral facial palsy with painful vesicles of the ear canal/auricle or oropharynx.
fields.etiology: Reactivated varicella-zoster virus (herpes zoster oticus).
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Peripheral facial palsy; [[★ painful vesicles of the ear canal]], auricle or oropharynx; hearing loss, tinnitus or vertigo; can cause eye damage, permanent hearing changes and altered taste.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; evaluate urgently for otic and neurologic disease.
fields.treatment: Antiviral therapy plus a systemic corticosteroid, started early when not contraindicated; urgent ear, nose and throat or neurology evaluation; protect the cornea if eyelid closure is impaired.

fields.name: Herpes simplex virus infection (also: HSV-1 and HSV-2)
fields.definition: Lifelong latent HSV (herpes simplex virus) infection with episodic reactivation, causing grouped vesicles and ulcers orally, genitally or anywhere on skin.
fields.etiology: HSV-1 or HSV-2 (Herpesviridae, double-stranded DNA); either type can cause oral or genital infection; spread by contact with oral/genital secretions or lesions, including asymptomatic shedding.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Reactivation triggers: stress, illness, menstruation, ultraviolet light exposure.
fields.pathology: Neurovirulent (invades and replicates in the nervous system), with latency and reactivation; HSV-1 genital infection recurs and sheds less often than HSV-2 genital infection.
fields.clinical: Prodrome of burning, pain or paresthesias ± tender lymphadenopathy, headache, fever; grouped vesicles on an erythematous base → shallow painful ulcers; dysuria in women with genital lesions; last up to two weeks, heal without scarring; first episode longer and worse than recurrences.
fields.diagnosis: Type-specific NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test)/PCR (nucleic acid amplification test/polymerase chain reaction) of a fresh vesicle, ulcer base or crust is preferred; culture less sensitive; a negative swab does not exclude; no HSV IgM (immunoglobulin M); no routine serologic screening. Differential: chancroid, syphilis (usually painless).
fields.treatment: Treat every first episode with oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir; recurrent genital: episodic or daily suppressive therapy; suppressive valacyclovir lowers HSV-2 transmission; condoms reduce risk; avoid contact during prodrome or lesions; topical antivirals give minimal benefit.

fields.name: Herpetic whitlow
fields.definition: Painful HSV (herpes simplex virus) infection of the distal finger or thumb.
fields.etiology: HSV-1 or HSV-2, often inoculated through broken skin; highly contagious through skin contact.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Prodromal burning/tingling, then grouped vesicles on an erythematous, swollen digit near the nailbed; fever or lymphangitis may occur.
fields.diagnosis: Confirm atypical cases with HSV NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test)/PCR (nucleic acid amplification test/polymerase chain reaction) from a fresh vesicle or lesion base; mimics bacterial felon/paronychia, contact dermatitis, blistering dactylitis.
fields.treatment: Do not incise and drain (delays healing); early oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir; suppression for frequent recurrence; treat bacterial superinfection only if present; cover lesions, hand hygiene.

fields.name: Molluscum contagiosum
fields.definition: Benign poxvirus skin infection producing smooth, dome-shaped, centrally umbilicated papules.
fields.etiology: Poxvirus spread by direct skin contact, shared contaminated objects and autoinoculation; sexual contact is common in adults with genital lesions.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Immunosuppression (more numerous, larger or atypical lesions).
fields.pathology: Most immunocompetent patients clear it spontaneously, though resolution may take months to several years.
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic, tender or pruritic; discrete, smooth, firm, flesh-colored, dome-shaped pearly papules averaging 3–5 mm; central umbilication is characteristic.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy if uncertain. Genital lesions: assess teens/adults for STIs (sexually transmitted infections); in a child, location alone does not prove abuse. Extensive/giant facial lesions: evaluate for immunosuppression including HIV (human immunodeficiency virus). Differential: basal cell carcinoma, sebaceous hyperplasia, condyloma acuminata.
fields.treatment: Observation for many; berdazimer 10.3% gel at home (age ≥1 year) or clinician-applied cantharidin 0.7% (age ≥2 years); curettage or cryotherapy; topical retinoids off label; treat associated dermatitis.

fields.name: Verruca vulgaris (also: common warts)
fields.definition: Common wart: benign proliferation of skin caused by HPV (human papillomavirus).
fields.etiology: HPV infection of keratinocytes; spread by skin-to-skin contact, autoinoculation and contaminated surfaces.
fields.epidemiology: Frequently ages 5–20 years.
fields.risk_factors: Nail biting (periungual, lip and tongue warts).
fields.pathology: Confined to the epidermis but expands and displaces the dermis, so it appears deeper; no roots (round, smooth underside); spontaneous resolution is the natural history.
fields.clinical: Usually on the hands (fingers/palms); usually < 1 cm, elevated round papules with a rough, grayish surface; tiny red/black dots (thrombosed dilated capillaries) that trimming makes more prominent.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy generally unnecessary, but for immunocompromised patients or uncertain lesions (ruling out squamous cell carcinoma). Differential: squamous cell carcinoma, molluscum contagiosum, seborrheic keratosis.
fields.treatment: Observation (many resolve); salicylic acid; cryotherapy every 2–3 weeks (pain, blistering, pigment change); no therapy eradicates HPV (human papillomavirus) with certainty; refer periungual, facial, extensive, recalcitrant or atypical lesions.

fields.name: Verruca plana (also: flat warts)
fields.definition: Flat warts: multiple smooth, slightly elevated, flat-topped papules caused by HPV (human papillomavirus).
fields.etiology: HPV infection of keratinocytes; spread by skin contact and autoinoculation.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Shaving spreads lesions through autoinoculation.
fields.pathology: HPV proliferation confined to the epidermis; spontaneous resolution is common.
fields.clinical: Multiple smooth, slightly elevated, flat-topped, skin-colored to light-brown papules on the face, forehead, dorsal hands and shins.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy for immunocompromised patients or lesions of uncertain etiology.
fields.treatment: Observation is reasonable; carefully selected salicylic acid, topical retinoids or cryotherapy, balanced against dyspigmentation and scarring risk; refer facial or extensive cases.

fields.name: Verruca plantaris (also: plantar warts)
fields.definition: HPV (human papillomavirus) wart on the weight-bearing surface of the foot.
fields.etiology: HPV infection of keratinocytes; spread by skin contact, autoinoculation and contaminated surfaces.
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Confined to the epidermis with no roots, though it displaces the dermis and looks deeper.
fields.clinical: Wart on a weight-bearing surface; may cluster into a mosaic wart (cluster of many warts).
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy only if uncertain or immunocompromised. Differential: squamous cell carcinoma, molluscum contagiosum, seborrheic keratosis.
fields.treatment: No therapy unless painful; salicylic acid 40%; cryotherapy.
