fields.name: Clavus (corn) (also: clavi; hard corn (clavus durum); soft corn (clavus mollum))
fields.definition: Localized, well-defined hyperkeratotic papule from focal pressure, with a hard central keratin core; hard and soft types
fields.etiology: Mechanical trauma to the skin, e.g. ill-fitting shoes; pressure on a localized area
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Tight or loose shoes, high heels; shoes without socks; walking barefoot; tools (hammer, rake) or sports equipment (tennis racket) rubbing the skin
fields.pathology: Focal pressure causes hyperkeratosis (thickened stratum corneum) with a central cone-shaped core of hard keratin pointing into the skin
fields.clinical: Hard corn: dorsal/lateral fifth toe, hyperkeratotic papules; soft corn: 4th-5th toe web space, soft from moisture maceration; well defined, <1.5 cm; pain with direct downward pressure; skin lines run through
fields.diagnosis: Distinguished by central hyperkeratotic core, pain on downward pressure, skin lines run through; vs wart (verruca vulgaris, human papillomavirus): interrupts skin lines, blackened center, pain with side pressure
fields.treatment: Padding; avoid poorly fitting footwear; over-the-counter keratolytics (salicylic acid pads, liquids, plasters); diabetic patient: refer to podiatry; well-fitting shoes and socks, no barefoot walking, shoe pads

fields.name: Callus (also: calluses)
fields.definition: Diffuse hyperkeratotic thickening from broad-area pressure or friction; no central core; larger than a corn
fields.etiology: Broad area of skin pressure/friction
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Tight or loose shoes, high heels; shoes without socks; walking barefoot; tools (hammer, rake) or sports equipment (tennis racket) rubbing the skin
fields.pathology: Pressure/friction leads to hyperkeratosis with diffuse thickening and no central core; acute, severe process forms a blister
fields.clinical: Palms of hands or balls of feet; painless; poorly defined, irregular shape; larger than a corn; skin lines run through
fields.diagnosis: Larger, irregular, usually painless, skin lines run through; vs corn (central core, pain on downward pressure) and wart (interrupts skin lines, not specific to pressure areas)
fields.treatment: Padding; avoid poorly fitting footwear; over-the-counter keratolytics (salicylic acid pads, liquids, plasters); diabetic patient: refer to podiatry; well-fitting shoes and socks, no barefoot walking, shoe pads

fields.name: Keloid
fields.definition: Fibroproliferative overgrowth of dense scar tissue extending beyond the original wound site; does not regress and tends to recur
fields.etiology: Abnormal wound healing (loss of the control mechanisms balancing repair) after surgical incisions, traumatic wounds, vaccination sites, burns, chickenpox, acne, or even minor scratches
fields.epidemiology: Rare incidence; associated with dark skin color; populations at risk: African American, Hispanic, Asian
fields.risk_factors: African American, Hispanic, or Asian ancestry; ear piercing and other cosmetic procedures in high-risk patients; acne (early treatment favors scar-free healing)
fields.pathology: Mechanism unclear; overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue; develops slowly and keeps enlarging for months to years; no regression with time
fields.clinical: May appear months after trauma; asymptomatic or pruritic/burning pain; cosmetic concern; firm bulbous nodules or markedly elevated plaques beyond wound margins; ear lobe, shoulders, sternal notch; rarely across joints
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy only if clinical doubt (may induce new scarring); differential: hypertrophic scar, dermatofibroma, foreign-body granuloma
fields.treatment: Prevention most important (high-risk: avoid piercings); combination therapy works best: silicone gel sheets, compression, intralesional steroids, cryotherapy, laser, intralesional 5-fluorouracil; excision (50-100% recurrence, often larger; keloids often worsened by surgery) then steroid injections or radiation

fields.name: Hypertrophic scar
fields.definition: Raised scar from abnormal wound healing that stays confined to the wound margins and regresses with time
fields.etiology: Abnormal wound healing (loss of the control mechanisms balancing repair) after surgery or injury
fields.epidemiology: Frequent incidence; no association with skin color
fields.risk_factors: Scars that cross joints or skin creases at a right angle
fields.pathology: Active proliferative phase of wound healing; develops rapidly within 4 weeks; stable, then regresses (flattens)
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic; develops soon after surgery, within 4 weeks of the event; confined to wound site margins; improves with time
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy only if clinical doubt (may induce new scarring); differential: keloid, dermatofibroma, foreign-body granuloma
fields.treatment: Intralesional corticosteroid or 5-fluorouracil; compression therapy and silicone sheeting; surgical excision (improves with appropriate surgery); pulsed dye laser reduces erythema by reducing neovascularization

fields.name: Cutaneous horn
fields.definition: Hard, conical, outward-growing keratin projection resembling an animal horn, arising from the surface of another lesion
fields.etiology: Arises from benign or malignant lesions: actinic keratosis, warts, seborrheic keratosis, keratoacanthoma, basal or squamous cell carcinoma
fields.epidemiology: Males = females; Caucasians over age 50; head, neck, upper extremities; common on sun-exposed areas (face, ears, hands)
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Composed of keratin (keratotic papule); the process at the base of the lesion is most important
fields.clinical: Possible bleeding and/or pain from trauma; papular or nodular base with firm hornlike protuberance; may be flat, keratotic, nodular, pedunculated, and/or ulcerated
fields.diagnosis: Often no clinical feature separates benign from malignant; deep shave biopsy samples the underlying lesion; differential: wart, actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: Depends on the underlying etiology; an underlying malignancy frequently needs excision per standard practice for tumor type and location

fields.name: Acrochordon (skin tag) (also: skin tag; fibroepithelial polyp)
fields.definition: Harmless soft, pedunculated growth of normal skin in areas of friction
fields.etiology: Forms where skin rubs together (friction)
fields.epidemiology: Very common: present in 60% of people by age 70; increased in females and obese patients
fields.risk_factors: Female sex; obesity/overweight; increasing age; friction areas
fields.pathology: Fibroepithelial pedunculated papilloma (polyp) with a narrow stalk and broad tip
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic; soft, pedunculated, skin-colored papules on a thin stalk, about 1-10 mm; neck, axilla, under the breasts, groin
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Usually for cosmesis: scissor excision, cryotherapy, or electrodesiccation; anesthesia not necessary; never cut or pull one off at home (bleeds); new tags may form in the same area

fields.name: Pressure injury (also: pressure ulcer; bedsore)
fields.definition: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue caused by unrelieved pressure
fields.etiology: Soft tissue compressed between a bony prominence and an external surface for a prolonged time; shear and friction (patient moved carelessly or sliding down in bed)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Prolonged unrelieved pressure damages underlying tissue; injury ranges from non-blanchable intact skin to deep ulcers extending to bone
fields.clinical: [[★ Stages 1-4]]: 1 non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; 2 partial-thickness loss, exposed dermis; 3 full-thickness loss, fat visible; 4 exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone; unstageable (obscured by slough/eschar); deep tissue (persistent non-blanchable deep red/purple)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical staging by depth of tissue loss; unstageable when slough or eschar hides the extent; frequent skin assessments
fields.treatment: Prevention is best: skin and nutrition assessment, clean dry skin, incontinence care, barrier creams, reposition every 2 hours, pain control, specialty (air) mattress; stage-based care, wound care specialist referral, infection control, silicone/hydrocolloid dressings, surgical debridement and closure

fields.name: Pilonidal cyst (also: pilonidal disease; pilonidal sinus)
fields.definition: Sac filled with hair and skin debris near the tailbone at the top of the gluteal cleft
fields.etiology: Acquired (once thought congenital): disrupted skin over the coccyx forms a pit that draws in hair and debris
fields.epidemiology: Male to female ratio 3:1; recurrence common
fields.risk_factors: Obesity; local trauma/irritation; sedentary lifestyle; increased hair density in the natal cleft; family history
fields.pathology: Pit causes follicular plugging; ingrown hairs block drainage and promote abscess; chronic disease forms sinus tracts (blind tracks)
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic, or abscess: sudden pain and swelling in the gluteal cleft, warm, tender, erythematous, fluctuant (wave-like fluid shift on palpation), purulent/bloody drainage; chronic: recurrent draining sinus openings, hair may protrude
fields.diagnosis: Diagnostic testing usually not needed
fields.treatment: Keep area clean and free of debris; shaving or laser hair therapy; incision and drainage for acute abscess; surgical referral for excision of chronic disease; hygiene education

fields.name: Dermatofibroma
fields.definition: Common benign firm dermal nodule (0.5-1 cm) formed by dense clusters of fibroblasts
fields.etiology: Uncertain; may form after trauma, viral infection, or insect bites
fields.epidemiology: Male to female 1:2; all races; legs (most common site) and arms; multiple (>15) lesions reported with systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), Down syndrome, Graves disease, leukemia
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Dermal fibroblasts form small dense clusters, creating a firm nodule
fields.clinical: Usually asymptomatic, often after an insect bite; slight pruritus or pain (most common painful skin tumor); firm nodule, brown halo, pink hue, raised scaly center; [[★ dimple sign]] (retracts beneath skin with lateral compression)
fields.diagnosis: Dermoscopy: peripheral pigment network with central white mass; differential: basal cell carcinoma, hypertrophic scar, melanoma, keratoacanthoma
fields.treatment: None unless diagnosis questioned or symptoms warrant; small lesions: shave or punch biopsy (diagnostic and therapeutic); larger lesions: surgical excision

fields.name: Keratoacanthoma
fields.definition: Rapidly growing dome-shaped tumor with a central keratin crater that often regresses spontaneously; histologically similar to squamous cell carcinoma
fields.etiology: Believed to arise from the pilosebaceous unit (hair follicle)
fields.epidemiology: Males > females; classically middle-aged, light-skinned people in hair-bearing, sun-exposed areas
fields.risk_factors: Age >40; sun exposure; very fair skin (always burns, never tans); male; tattoos (red ink); skin trauma (lasers, surgery, cryotherapy); human papillomavirus infection
fields.pathology: Histopathologically similar to squamous cell carcinoma, with strong arguments for classifying it as a variant of invasive squamous cell carcinoma; may keep growing or rarely metastasize
fields.clinical: Triphasic: rapid growth (6-8 weeks), stabilization, regression (after 3-6 months); solitary smooth shiny dome-shaped red papule/nodule with central keratin-filled crater (volcano)
fields.diagnosis: Biopsy: the only reliable method; differential: squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, amelanotic melanoma, molluscum contagiosum
fields.treatment: Excise or destroy (possible malignancy): elliptical excision with 5-mm margins; Mohs surgery for large, recurrent, or cosmetically/functionally sensitive sites; intralesional methotrexate before excision to shrink it

fields.name: Epidermoid (epidermal) cyst (also: epidermal inclusion cyst; improperly called sebaceous cyst)
fields.definition: Most common cutaneous cyst: epithelium enclosed within the dermis and filled with keratin
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Males > females (2:1); very common; face, scalp, neck, trunk
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Cystic enclosure of epithelium in the dermis filled with keratin; looks like sebum but is keratin, so not a sebaceous cyst; fibrous capsule
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic or drains foul-smelling material; single firm, moveable, round nodule with central pore (punctum); expresses cream-colored pasty material smelling of rancid cheese
fields.diagnosis: Lab tests usually unnecessary; differential: cystic acne, lipoma, neurofibroma, keratoacanthoma, basal cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: Asymptomatic: none; inflamed: postpone excision a few weeks, intralesional triamcinolone, antibiotics if needed; surgical removal of the entire capsule when not inflamed; small (1-3 cm): punch incision and removal of contents

fields.name: Syringoma
fields.definition: Benign neoplasm of the eccrine (sweat gland) ducts, forming small papules around the eyes
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Appears at puberty; females > males
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Benign neoplastic growth of eccrine sweat ducts
fields.clinical: Usually asymptomatic; multiple 1-2 mm skin-colored, pink or brown papules, mostly on the eyelids (periorbital) and upper cheeks
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; biopsy if malignancy concern; differential: milia, xanthelasma, basal cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: Cosmetic only: oral isotretinoin (higher recurrence risk); curettage and electrodesiccation, laser, cryotherapy, or excision (possible poor cosmetic results)

fields.name: Infantile hemangioma (also: hemangioma of infancy; superficial type formerly called strawberry hemangioma)
fields.definition: Congenital benign vascular neoplasm; most common tumor of infancy, with rapid proliferation then slow involution
fields.etiology: Mutations of genes regulating endothelial cell proliferation
fields.epidemiology: Noticed in first days to weeks of life; more common in preterm infants, females (3:1), Caucasians; head and neck 60%, trunk 25%, extremities 15%
fields.risk_factors: Prematurity; female sex; Caucasian; history probes low birth weight, multiple gestation, placental abnormalities, family history
fields.pathology: Rapid endothelial proliferation; superficial (most common): dilated dermal vessels, bright red papule/plaque/nodule; deep (least common): deep dermis/subcutis, pale, skin-colored or blue nodule
fields.clinical: Half present at birth; earliest sign blanching, then fine telangiectasias, then red macule; rapid growth in the neonatal period, most growth in the first 4-6 months, slowing at 6-12 months; involution 50% by age 5, 70% by 7, 90% by 9; may block vision, feeding, breathing, or ear canal
fields.diagnosis: Mostly clinical; refer to a vascular anomalies specialist if in doubt; differential: nevus flammeus, pyogenic granuloma; 5 or more skin lesions may be associated with hepatic hemangiomas
fields.treatment: Often none (serial observation); treat for cosmetic, functional, ulceration, or infection reasons: beta-blockers first line (oral propranolol, topical timolol); corticosteroids (also listed as first line; topical, intralesional, oral) slow growth and shrink proliferating lesions; pulsed dye laser; surgical excision

fields.name: Nevus flammeus (also: port-wine stain)
fields.definition: Congenital vascular lesion of dilated dermal capillaries, present at birth and persisting for life
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: More common in Caucasians; male = female; present at birth
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Dilated superficial dermal capillaries through the entire depth of the dermis; no endothelial proliferation; grows with the child, no involution
fields.clinical: Early: flat, well-circumscribed, blanchable pink-to-purple patches, darker with crying, fever, or heat, usually unilateral with sharp midline cutoff; later darker, thickened, raised plaque; psychosocial burden; forehead/upper eyelid stain may mark Sturge-Weber syndrome
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: No treatment required; tinted waterproof makeup; pulsed dye laser (selective vessel destruction via intravascular coagulation, later replaced by collagen)

fields.name: Nevus simplex (also: stork bite)
fields.definition: Congenital vascular lesion; a more superficial variant of nevus flammeus
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Dermal capillaries, more superficial than nevus flammeus
fields.clinical: Present at birth; more noticeable with crying; pink to erythematous, irregular, blanchable macules/patches, single or multiple; most common on head and neck
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Expectant: fades within 1 year, or may persist for life (neck)

fields.name: Cherry angioma (also: senile angioma)
fields.definition: Very common acquired vascular papule formed by capillary (venule) proliferation, increasing with age
fields.etiology: Unknown
fields.epidemiology: Very common; occurs with increasing age
fields.risk_factors: Increasing age
fields.pathology: Capillary (venule) proliferation
fields.clinical: Most common on the trunk; may bleed after trauma; smooth, firm, deep red papules <5 mm that [[★ blanch with pressure]] (may not blanch completely if fibrotic)
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not necessary unless bothersome; new lesions will develop and cannot be prevented; laser for superficial lesions; shave excision and electrocautery for large lesions

fields.name: Telangiectasia
fields.definition: Acquired vascular lesion: a permanently dilated capillary (<1 mm)
fields.etiology: Primary or secondary; associated with numerous diseases
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Blanchable; single, in groups, or with a central punctum
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Nevus araneus (spider angioma) (also: spider angioma)
fields.definition: Acquired vascular lesion from dilation of preexisting vessels, without vascular proliferation
fields.etiology: Estrogen excess states
fields.epidemiology: Hands and fingers in children; face, neck, upper trunk, and arms in adults
fields.risk_factors: Pregnancy; birth control pills; cirrhosis, liver failure; history should cover hormone use, alcohol, liver-toxic medications
fields.pathology: No vascular proliferation; dilation of preexisting vessels (arterioles on the body)
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic; solitary or multiple lesions <10 mm; lesion blanches
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: None may be needed; pregnancy- and pill-related lesions resolve after delivery or stopping; pulsed dye laser resolves most lesions

fields.name: Pyogenic granuloma
fields.definition: Benign, rapidly growing vascular tumor of skin and mucous membranes; misnamed, as it is neither infectious nor granulomatous
fields.etiology: Exact cause unknown; response to irritation, injury/trauma, or hormonal changes
fields.epidemiology: Common in children, young adults, and pregnancy
fields.risk_factors: Trauma to the area; pregnancy/hormonal factors
fields.pathology: Acquired overgrowth of blood vessels in skin/mucous membranes
fields.clinical: Head, neck, fingers; rapid growth, painless, bleeds spontaneously or after irritation; bright red exophytic papule/nodule, moist surface, epithelial collarette base; average 6.5 mm; may erode, ulcerate, crust
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; differential: cherry angioma, malignant melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: May resolve spontaneously (pregnancy-related often after delivery); for cosmesis or bleeding: surgical excision (histology, lowest recurrence, most scarring); shave with curettage and electrodesiccation, laser, cryotherapy; early follow-up if it recurs

fields.name: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (also: von Recklinghausen disease)
fields.definition: Common neurocutaneous genetic disorder causing tumors on nerve tissue; also called [[★ von Recklinghausen disease]]
fields.etiology: NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gene on chromosome 17; [[★ three types]]: NF1, NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2; NF2 gene, chromosome 22), schwannomatosis or NF3 (SMARCB1 and LZTR1 genes, chromosome 22)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Cutaneous neurofibromas: benign nerve sheath tumors from peripheral nerves; plexiform neurofibromas: large tumors in tissue covering nerves, anywhere except brain and spinal cord, may be locally invasive
fields.clinical: Café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal; often first sign, at birth or first year); cutaneous neurofibromas from puberty, more with age; Crowe sign (grouped axillary/inguinal freckles <5 mm, more prominent with sun); plexiform neurofibromas
fields.diagnosis: Six or more café-au-lait spots are diagnostic, but the macules alone do not establish the diagnosis; axillary/inguinal freckling is a criterion (under-breast site is not)
fields.treatment: Surveillance: skin exam at each visit for new or progressing neurofibromas; evaluate the extent of plexiform lesions; national and regional support groups

fields.name: Xanthelasma
fields.definition: Soft, yellow cholesterol plaques, most often on the medial eyelids
fields.etiology: Associated with lipid disorders
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Collection of lipid-laden macrophages
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic; soft yellow plaques; most common location medial eyelids
fields.diagnosis: Screen for hyperlipidemia; may signify increased risk of cardiac disease
fields.treatment: Laser or surgical excision; recurrence common

fields.name: Lipoma
fields.definition: Most common soft tissue tumor: benign localized overgrowth of fat cells in subcutaneous tissue
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Most common soft tissue tumor
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Benign localized overgrowth of fat cells in subcutaneous tissue; single or multiple tumors
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic unless adjoining structures invaded; anywhere on the body; soft, painless, rubbery subcutaneous nodules, usually <5 cm
fields.diagnosis: Typically clinical; differential: epidermal cyst, dermatofibroma, abscess
fields.treatment: Observe asymptomatic tumors; excise cosmetically deforming enlarging masses or those with uncertain diagnosis

fields.name: Digital mucous cyst (also: mucous cyst)
fields.definition: Pseudo-cyst on the distal digit without a true cellular lining, formed by mucin extruded from a joint
fields.etiology: Extrusion of mucinous contents from a local joint space into the surrounding dermis
fields.epidemiology: Females > males
fields.risk_factors: Osteoarthritis
fields.pathology: No cellular lining (true capsule); collecting mucin compacts dermal cells at the margin, mimicking a capsule
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic unless large; translucent skin-colored cystic papule, typically over the distal interphalangeal joint, over the proximal nail matrix or nail bed; may cause a longitudinal nail groove
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Observe asymptomatic lesions; excise symptomatic cysts or those causing nail dystrophy

fields.name: Sebaceous hyperplasia
fields.definition: Common benign enlargement of sebaceous glands with no known potential for malignant transformation
fields.etiology: Aging slows turnover of sebocytes (sebum-producing cells)
fields.epidemiology: Common
fields.risk_factors: Increasing age; immunosuppression (high risk)
fields.pathology: Slowed sebocyte turnover crowds the gland, which enlarges
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic, cosmetic or malignancy concern; single or multiple soft whitish-yellow or skin-colored papules 2-9 mm with central umbilication (sebum may be expressed); common on the face
fields.diagnosis: Dermoscopy distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma; biopsy if malignancy concern; differential: basal cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: Treatment not required; lesions tend to recur and treatment risks scarring; light electrocautery

lectures.title: Pigmented Skin Lesions
lectures.deck: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx

fields.name: Ephelides (also: freckles)
fields.definition: Freckles: small, light brown, symmetric macules on (mostly) sun-exposed skin
fields.etiology: Autosomal dominant; related to mutation in the MCR-1 gene (the receptor for alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone); carriers are at high risk of developing freckles
fields.epidemiology: Fair-skinned people, often blonde or red hair, possibly Celtic ancestry; male = female; first appear in young children
fields.risk_factors: Fair skin; MCR-1 gene mutation carriers; ultraviolet exposure darkens them
fields.pathology: Decreased MCR-1 pathway activity (via cyclic adenosine monophosphate) favors pheomelanin (yellow/red, sulfur-containing pigment); biopsy: normal to reduced number of hypertrophic melanocytes with increased melanin in basal epidermis
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic 3-5 mm light brown macules, may become confluent; darken with sun (spring/summer), fade with cessation of sun exposure (winter); regress later in life
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; lentigines are the main differential diagnosis
fields.treatment: Sun protection with patient education/counseling; topical depigmenting agents (hydroquinone, retinoids, alpha-hydroxy acids, botanicals); intense pulsed light or lasers preferred (may relapse); no cryotherapy (lesions too small)

fields.name: Lentigines (lentigo simplex) (also: age spots; simple lentigo)
fields.definition: Common benign melanocytic lesion; types: lentigo simplex, acral, agminated, generalized
fields.etiology: Not well known; possibly disrupted melanocyte homeostasis from increased melanocyte density; dysregulated melanization
fields.epidemiology: Bimodal age distribution: early childhood or later in life
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Increased melanocyte density; melanin macroglobules; lentigo simplex lacks the mutations found in solar lentigo, PUVA (psoralen plus ultraviolet A) lentigines and common acquired nevi
fields.clinical: Well-circumscribed, round to oval, uniformly black or brown macules <5 mm; skin, conjunctiva, mucocutaneous surfaces; sun-exposed and protected sites; do not fade without sun; agminated = grouped light brown macules; partial/generalized lentigo raises concern for an inherited syndrome
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis
fields.treatment: Treatment not necessary; cosmetic removal if preferred: cryotherapy or quality-switched laser

fields.name: Solar lentigo
fields.definition: Benign accumulation of pigment-producing cells from cumulative ultraviolet exposure; architecturally distinct from melanocytic nevi
fields.etiology: Chronic ultraviolet exposure: UVB (ultraviolet B) stimulates melanocyte proliferation; UVA (ultraviolet A) causes oxidative damage to melanin and DNA; PUVA (psoralen plus ultraviolet A) therapy causes a variant
fields.epidemiology: Older age (90% at age 50; >90% of white patients over 70); white skin (Fitzpatrick I-III) and Asians
fields.risk_factors: Older age, sun damage/cumulative ultraviolet dose, ephelides, tanning (tanning beds), birth control use; PUVA lentigines: number of treatments, male sex, fair skin, older age
fields.pathology: Proliferation of basal melanocytes with increased melanin production; keratinocytes stimulate melanocytes by paracrine signaling
fields.clinical: Light to dark brown macules, <1 mm to several cm, well defined with irregular borders, may coalesce at severe-sunburn sites; face, dorsal forearms/hands; PUVA type also on buttocks/genitalia; over time enlarge/darken, stay stable, regress or become lichenoid keratoses; associated with actinic keratosis, squamous/basal cell carcinoma, melanoma
fields.diagnosis: Dermoscopy: finger-like projections, "moth-eaten" border; biopsy if atypical or uncertain, especially to exclude lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ)
fields.treatment: Treatment not necessary; cosmetic: retinoids, cryotherapy (first-line office treatment), quality-switched laser, peels; daily broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF (sun protection factor) 30 or more; annual skin exam

fields.name: Seborrheic keratosis
fields.definition: Benign beige to brown to black papules and plaques
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Common in older adults
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: 2-20 mm; velvety or warty feel; "stuck on" or pasted-on appearance; easily mistaken for neoplasms
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis
fields.treatment: Supportive; cryotherapy may help if itchy or inflamed (lesions recur after treatment)

fields.name: Dermatosis papulosa nigrans
fields.definition: Multiple small black or dark brown papules on the face and neck, identical to small seborrheic keratoses
fields.etiology: Likely genetic
fields.epidemiology: Common in African Americans, dark-skinned Asians and Polynesians; female > male
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Believed to be a developmental defect of the hair follicle
fields.clinical: Multiple smooth, firm, 1-5 mm black or dark brown papules on face and neck
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; biopsy if uncertain
fields.treatment: Best left untreated; excision, curettage or laser if needed; avoid cryotherapy (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation)

fields.name: Vitiligo
fields.definition: Common autoimmune skin disease causing depigmentation; nonsegmental and segmental forms
fields.etiology: Autoimmune: T cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes
fields.epidemiology: Any age; usually starts before the 30s (half before 20s, one-third before age 12); male = female
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: T cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes causes depigmentation
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic white, non-scaly macules/patches with distinct margins, usually symmetric; face (periorificial), acral, genital sites first; segmental = unilateral, block-like, not crossing midline; unpredictable flares; psychological burden; associated with other conditions
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; Wood lamp exam in a dark room (lesions fluoresce); labs for associated autoimmune disease: CBC (complete blood count), antinuclear antibody
fields.treatment: <5% body surface area: topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus; face/neck/intertriginous/children); >5%: narrowband UVB (ultraviolet B) phototherapy first line; topical + phototherapy ideal; psychological support; grafting only for stable disease

fields.name: Congenital melanocytic nevus
fields.definition: Pigmented neoplasm of melanocytes evident at birth or shortly after; small, medium or large; high risk of melanoma, rising with lesion size
fields.etiology: Somatic mutations
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Associated with neurofibromatosis type 1
fields.pathology: Arise from neural crest-derived melanocytic precursors that migrate along neurovascular bundles
fields.clinical: Flat brown patches or plaques, smooth or slightly uneven borders; pebbly, rugose, verrucous or lobular; trunk/extremities most often; nevi on head, neck, posterior midline: neurocutaneous melanosis (seizures, hydrocephalus, neurological deficits, vomiting; poor prognosis)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis, sometimes biopsy; cranial or axial lesions: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain ± total spine for neurocutaneous melanosis
fields.treatment: Individualized by melanoma risk, cosmetic and functional concerns; ideally surgical removal of as much nevus as possible; observation if little graft-site skin; counseling/support groups for large nevi

fields.name: Nevus spilus (also: spotted nevus)
fields.definition: Spotted nevus; a variant of congenital nevus; rarely progresses to melanoma
fields.etiology: Possibly a somatic mutation
fields.epidemiology: Present at birth or in the first years of life
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Café-au-lait-like tan background (<1 cm to >10 cm) with scattered superimposed darker macules or papules; trunk and extremities; associated with vascular, central nervous system or connective tissue anomalies
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Observation with periodic clinical evaluation; sun protection counseling

fields.name: Common acquired melanocytic nevus (also: mole)
fields.definition: Mole: benign melanocytic neoplasm arising after birth
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Develop slowly after birth; number peaks in the 30s then declines; more numerous in light-skinned people who sunburn easily
fields.risk_factors: Ultraviolet radiation exposure, male sex, some genetic component
fields.pathology: Arise from junctional melanocytes; junctional and compound nevi
fields.clinical: Usually <6 mm, round to oval, sharply demarcated, homogeneous surface and color (skin-colored, brown, pink); anywhere on body; enlarge symmetrically, stabilize, regress; very dark brown/black in light skin is suspicious
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis
fields.treatment: Observation; removal for cosmetic or symptomatic relief; sun protection counseling

fields.name: Blue nevus
fields.definition: Group of lesions of deeply pigmented spindle or epithelioid melanocytes in the dermis: common, cellular, combined and atypical cellular blue nevi
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Women > men; most common in the 20s; common type arises in adolescence, cellular type before age 40
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Deeply pigmented spindle or epithelioid melanocytes located in the dermis
fields.clinical: Single blue, blue-gray or blue-black macule/papule; dorsal hands/feet, scalp, buttocks, sacrum; common <1 cm, cellular >1 cm plaques or nodules
fields.diagnosis: Clinical for small lesions; biopsy for larger lesions
fields.treatment: Observation; biopsy/excision if changes noted

fields.name: Pigmented spindle cell nevus (also: Reed nevus)
fields.definition: Benign, sharply circumscribed, darkly pigmented papule
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Commonly in the 30s; female > male
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Jet-black papule (may show blue, gray or brown), usually <7 mm; extremities, mainly lower, especially the thigh
fields.diagnosis: Confirm with biopsy
fields.treatment: [[★ Excision with negative margins]]

fields.name: Spitz nevus
fields.definition: Usually benign nevus with a growth phase (fast or slow) followed by a stable period
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Solitary, asymptomatic, pink/red, hairless, firm, dome-shaped; [[★ sometimes resembles melanoma]]; mm to cm; face, neck, trunk, extremities, sparing palms/soles/mucous membranes; multiple lesions can signal a familial cancer syndrome
fields.diagnosis: Biopsy vs [[★ wide excision]]
fields.treatment: Excision

fields.name: Dysplastic melanocytic nevus
fields.definition: Nevus with atypical architectural and cytologic features; may progress to melanoma (more nevi, higher risk)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Common in Caucasians
fields.risk_factors: Family history; dysplastic nevus syndrome can give over 100 nevi by adolescence
fields.pathology: Atypical architectural and cytologic features
fields.clinical: At least 5 mm with irregular, indistinct borders; variable tan to brown pigment; smooth or "pebbly" surface; sun-exposed skin
fields.diagnosis: Biopsy
fields.treatment: Observation; biopsy all changing or developing lesions; excision if concern for melanoma; sun protection

lectures.title: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions
lectures.deck: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx

fields.name: Actinic keratosis (also: solar keratosis)
fields.definition: Premalignant rough, scaly patch or bump caused by UV (ultraviolet) damage; lies on a continuum with keratinocyte carcinoma, and some turn into squamous cell carcinoma.
fields.etiology: Chronic cumulative UV (ultraviolet) injury → dysplastic keratinocytes in a field of sun-damaged skin; UV-induced TP53 mutations are the critical molecular event.
fields.epidemiology: Fair-complexioned people, sun-exposed skin; most common precancerous skin lesion worldwide; up to 60% of men over 60 in high-UV (ultraviolet) climates.
fields.risk_factors: Advanced age; cumulative UV (ultraviolet) exposure, outdoor work or recreation; prior actinic keratosis or keratinocyte carcinoma; male sex/bald scalp; immunosuppression (transplant recipients 65× risk).
fields.pathology: Intraepidermal keratinocytic dysplasia; field cancerization (surrounding normal-looking skin carries subclinical mutations); ~1 in 1,000 lesions per year progresses to squamous cell carcinoma (Lecture 3 instead gives 0.025–16% per lesion per year), cumulative field risk matters more.
fields.clinical: 0.2–0.6 cm flesh-colored, pink, or slightly hyperpigmented papules with sandpaper texture, often felt more than seen; face, scalp, ears, forearms, dorsal hands; may be tender. Bleeding, induration, ulceration, rapid growth are not typical.
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical ± dermoscopy; shave or punch biopsy if concerning for squamous cell carcinoma or persists/recurs after therapy; key call: actinic keratosis vs squamous cell carcinoma in situ vs invasive. Differential: early squamous cell carcinoma (most important), superficial basal cell carcinoma, seborrheic keratosis, solar lentigo, verruca.
fields.treatment: Few lesions: liquid nitrogen cryotherapy (crusts, clears in 10–14 days). Multiple lesions in one area: field therapy, topical fluorouracil most effective; imiquimod; photodynamic therapy. Daily sun protection; refer for uncertainty, high burden, recurrence, immunosuppression.

fields.name: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (also: SCC in situ = Bowen disease)
fields.definition: Second most common skin cancer, arising in the flat squamous cells of the outer skin layer; in situ form is Bowen disease. Almost always easy to cure when found early.
fields.etiology: Long-term UV (ultraviolet) damage from sun or tanning beds; may arise from an actinic keratosis.
fields.epidemiology: Mainly fair-skinned people who burn easily, on exposed sites; common and often aggressive in organ transplant recipients (multiple tumors ~5 years after transplant).
fields.risk_factors: Prolonged cumulative sun exposure; immunosuppression (transplant, CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia), HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)/AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome), iatrogenic); chronic wounds, scars, prior radiation fields; certain genetic diseases.
fields.pathology: Pathology grades differentiation, depth, perineural/perivascular invasion, margins, aggressive subtype. High-risk sites (lip, ear, scalp, temple, nose, genitalia, mucosa) and >10 tumors raise recurrence/metastasis; metastatic rate 3–7% when sun-induced.
fields.clinical: Small red, conical, hard nodule that may ulcerate; or nonhealing ulcer, warty nodule, pink plaque with hemorrhagic crust. Red flags: rapid growth, pain, bleeding, induration, fixation, palpable nodes.
fields.diagnosis: Shave, punch, or excisional biopsy deep enough to separate in situ from invasive; palpate draining nodes; imaging/nodal evaluation for high-risk tumors. Differential: actinic keratosis, keratoacanthoma, verruca, basal cell carcinoma.
fields.treatment: In situ: imiquimod, topical fluorouracil, or curettage and electrodesiccation. Invasive: surgical excision or Mohs surgery (high-risk sites, recurrent, >1 cm face/>2 cm trunk or extremities, immunosuppressed). Advanced: PD-1 (programmed cell death protein 1) blockade, cetuximab. Nicotinamide cuts new tumors ~30% in high-risk patients.

fields.name: Basal cell carcinoma
fields.definition: The most common form of cancer; slow-growing and highly curable early, but capable of significant local destruction; often a shiny bump or a sore that does not heal.
fields.etiology: UV (ultraviolet) light drives carcinogenesis in sun-exposed skin; sun exposure is the main cause.
fields.epidemiology: Most common cancer; fair-skinned people with intense, intermittent sun exposure; a second basal cell carcinoma develops in up to 50%.
fields.risk_factors: Intense intermittent UV (ultraviolet) exposure, fair skin; immunosuppression (non-Hodgkin lymphoma, solid-organ transplant, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant) raises incidence and recurrence.
fields.pathology: Histologic subtypes: superficial, nodular, micronodular, infiltrative; subtype dictates behavior and treatment. Morpheaform, micronodular, and infiltrative are aggressive. Metastasis rare but serious.
fields.clinical: Nodular: pearly papule with central erosion and telangiectasias (seen better on stretching). Pigmented: mimics melanoma. Superficial: red, shiny, scaly thin plaques on back/chest. Morpheaform: ivory-white, scar-like, subclinical spread.
fields.diagnosis: Shave or punch biopsy confirms and gives histologic subtype (low vs high risk); no routine imaging for localized disease. Differential: sebaceous hyperplasia, nevus, squamous cell carcinoma.
fields.treatment: Curettage and electrodesiccation, excision (≤5% recurrence), or Mohs (~98% cure; eyelids, nasolabial folds, canthi, external ear, temple, recurrent, aggressive histology). Superficial: imiquimod or topical fluorouracil. Advanced: hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib). Annual full-skin exam.

fields.name: Malignant melanoma
fields.definition: Malignant melanocytic skin cancer; the leading cause of death due to skin disease.
fields.etiology: UV (ultraviolet) exposure and sunburn; fewer than 30% arise from an existing mole, most arise de novo; acral lentiginous type is not clearly UV-driven.
fields.epidemiology: 4th most common cancer in the U.S.; incidence doubled over 30 years; lifetime risk ~2% in white individuals vs 0.1–0.5% in skin of color; 1 in 4 before age 40; men over 70 especially affected.
fields.risk_factors: UV (ultraviolet) exposure/sunburn history, fair phenotype, numerous or atypical nevi, personal or family history, immunosuppression.
fields.pathology: Subtypes: superficial spreading (~2/3; radial then vertical growth), lentigo maligna (older, chronic sun), nodular (rapid, often amelanotic), acral lentiginous (palms, soles, nails), ocular, mucosal. Breslow thickness = most important prognostic factor.
fields.clinical: ABCDE: Asymmetry, irregular Border, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (most important). Ugly duckling sign (a lesion unlike the patient's other nevi). Acral: dark irregular palm/sole lesion or new broad nail streak.
fields.diagnosis: Excisional biopsy allowing full-thickness depth; report Breslow, ulceration, margins, mitoses. Sentinel lymph node biopsy at ≥1.0 mm (≥0.8 mm with risk features); BRAF testing. Staging: [[★ 0 epidermis only, I–II localized, III nodes, IV other organs]].
fields.treatment: Re-excision margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm; <1 mm 1 cm; >1 mm 1–2 cm. [[★ Refer deeper than 1 mm]] or with spread to an expert center. Advanced: BRAF-targeted therapy, immune checkpoint therapy (anti-PD-1, programmed cell death protein 1). Monthly self-exam (ABCDE), sun protection.
fields.mortality: Leading cause of death due to skin disease; ~7,990 U.S. deaths in 2023 (~two-thirds men); mortality declining (earlier detection, immunotherapy); survival drops sharply with Breslow thickness and nodal/distant spread.

fields.name: Kaposi sarcoma
fields.definition: Rare cancer of cells lining blood and lymph vessels, causing abnormal patches, spots, or lumps on skin, in the mouth, or in internal organs.
fields.etiology: HHV-8 (human herpesvirus 8) causes all forms, combined with a weakened immune system; host immune status shapes expression.
fields.epidemiology: Classic: older men. Endemic: young Black men in equatorial Africa. Iatrogenic: immunosuppressive therapy. Epidemic: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), falling with antiretroviral therapy. Fifth form: HIV-negative men who have sex with men.
fields.risk_factors: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) immune deficiency; immunosuppressive therapy (transplant); age-related immune senescence; men who have sex with men.
fields.pathology: Vascular-lining cell tumor; five clinical forms: classic (chronic), endemic (often aggressive), iatrogenic (may improve as immunosuppression is reduced), epidemic, fifth form (indolent). Biopsy shows HHV-8 (human herpesvirus 8)-associated findings.
fields.clinical: Red or purple macules, plaques, nodules on skin or mucosa; hard palate lesions common (oral exam essential); marked edema even with few lesions; gastrointestinal (often silent) and pulmonary (dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis); may worsen on starting antiretrovirals (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome).
fields.diagnosis: Biopsy a representative lesion; HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) test, CD4 count, viral load; skin, oral, node, edema review; chest radiograph if pulmonary possible, bronchoscopy for suspected lung disease. Differential: bacillary angiomatosis, pyogenic granuloma.
fields.treatment: Epidemic: start/optimize antiretroviral therapy first. Iatrogenic: reduce immunosuppression (with transplant team). Classic: palliative intralesional vincristine, vinblastine, bleomycin, or radiation. Advanced: liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel.
fields.mortality: Classic: usually indolent and rarely fatal; endemic, visceral, or immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome disease can be aggressive and rapidly fatal.

fields.name: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (also: mycosis fungoides)
fields.definition: Rare non-Hodgkin lymphoma in which malignant T cells migrate to the skin, causing itchy, scaly patches, plaques, or tumors; may stay skin-confined for years or decades.
fields.etiology: No specific causative exposure is well defined.
fields.epidemiology: Rare; no established incidence rate; nondescript patches may be present >10 years before histologic confirmation.
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Malignant T-cell skin infiltrates (localized or generalized) before any systemic spread; may progress to Sézary syndrome (erythroderma with circulating malignant T cells).
fields.clinical: Erythematous patches or scaly plaques on the trunk, often >5 cm, mimicking psoriasis, eczema, or tinea; itch out of proportion to inflammation; follicular involvement with hair loss is a clue; advanced: tumors, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy.
fields.diagnosis: Skin biopsy, often repeated (one nondiagnostic biopsy does not exclude it); advanced: CBC (complete blood count) with differential, circulating Sézary cells, T-cell gene rearrangement, flow cytometry; node staging.
fields.treatment: Stage-directed, skin-first: topical corticosteroids, topical mechlorethamine, bexarotene gel, UV (ultraviolet) phototherapy. Progressive: PUVA (psoralen plus ultraviolet A), methotrexate, photopheresis, systemic bexarotene, romidepsin/vorinostat, total-skin electron beam.
fields.mortality: Survival not reduced in limited patch disease; tumors, erythroderma, nodes, and Sézary syndrome worsen prognosis; overly aggressive therapy may cause premature death.

fields.name: Nail unit melanoma
fields.definition: Rare acral melanoma of the nail unit, arising most often in the matrix.
fields.etiology: Not clearly UV (ultraviolet)-driven.
fields.epidemiology: May occur in any skin tone; thumb and great toe are high-yield sites.
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Matrix tumors produce longitudinal nail-plate bands (melanonychia); delayed recognition leads to advanced-stage presentation; outcome driven by stage, Breslow thickness, ulceration, spread.
fields.clinical: New or evolving longitudinal melanonychia in one digit: widening, irregular color/lines, proximal widening or triangular shape, blurred borders, dystrophy; Hutchinson sign (pigment extending onto the proximal nail fold); amelanotic form is red, pink, eroded.
fields.diagnosis: Onychoscopy; urgent referral for nail-unit biopsy sampling the site of origin (often the matrix). Differential: subungual hematoma, benign longitudinal melanonychia.
fields.treatment: Dermatology, nail surgery, surgical oncology; digit-sparing wide excision or Mohs with immunostaining; amputation only for deep, extensive, or bone-involving disease; staging per Breslow principles.

fields.name: Nail unit squamous cell carcinoma (also: nail unit Bowen disease)
fields.definition: Most common malignant nail tumor, including its in situ form (Bowen disease).
fields.etiology: Associated with high-risk HPV (human papillomavirus); periungual HPV-associated disease may be multifocal.
fields.epidemiology: Most common malignant nail tumor; older age.
fields.risk_factors: High-risk HPV (human papillomavirus), immunosuppression, chronic inflammation/trauma, prior radiation, older age.
fields.pathology: May be multifocal; can invade bone of the distal phalanx.
fields.clinical: Chronic unilateral verrucous periungual papule or plaque, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, oozing, bleeding, nail-plate destruction, longitudinal erythronychia, pain; often repeatedly labeled a wart, paronychia, or fungal infection.
fields.diagnosis: Refer for biopsy of the site of origin; KOH (potassium hydroxide), fungal culture, or PAS (periodic acid–Schiff) to rule out onychomycosis (a positive result does not exclude cancer); radiography/MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for bone extent.
fields.treatment: Margin-controlled surgery: Mohs or wide excision (limited destruction recurs more); amputation only for bone invasion or uncleared disease; avoid repeated empiric wart/antifungal treatment.

fields.name: Nail unit basal cell carcinoma
fields.definition: Basal cell carcinoma of the nail fold or bed.
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Exceptionally uncommon.
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Persistent ulcerated or pearly lesion of the nail fold or bed.
fields.diagnosis: Prompt referral for nail-unit biopsy sampling the site of origin; persistent ulceration or bleeding is an urgent referral trigger.
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Glomus tumor
fields.definition: Rare benign growth from glomus bodies (tiny structures controlling blood flow and body temperature), most often under the fingernails or in fingertips.
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Rare; most common under the fingernails or in the fingertips.
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Benign nail-unit neoplasm that can mimic malignancy.
fields.clinical: Classic triad: severe paroxysmal pain, exquisite point tenderness, cold sensitivity; small red-blue subungual focus; nail may look nearly normal.
fields.diagnosis: Triad strongly suggests it but does not replace imaging: ultrasound or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to localize an occult tumor.
fields.treatment: Surgical removal when symptomatic; excellent outcome after complete removal.

fields.definition: Non-cancerous, fast-growing red bump of abnormal blood vessels around the nail fold or under the nail plate.

fields.definition: Non-cancerous bony growth or spur under the fingernail or toenail, most commonly the big toe.
